sections.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Positive Social Norms

content.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Positive Social Norms
content.overview: This section provides a trauma-informed, practical guide to understanding the core purpose of positive social norms and how it shapes physical, emotional, and relational safety in daily family life. Designed for parents, caregivers, and family support practitioners, it focuses on realistic, repeatable steps that strengthen safety, predictability, and connection.
content.psychoeducation: Why does positive social norms matter in section 1? Children and families thrive on predictability, nervous-system safety, and attuned repair. When positive social norms is practised consistently, stress responses decrease and relational trust grows. Why positive social norms matters for child development.
learning_goals: Understand the purpose and value of positive social norms. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Positive Social Norms)
Identify common challenges and how to respond calmly. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Positive Social Norms)
Practice simple, repeatable strategies that build confidence. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Positive Social Norms)
Strengthen connection and emotional safety during difficult moments. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Positive Social Norms)
step_by_step: Pause & Ground: Notice your own breathing, body tension, and tone before addressing positive social norms.
Observe Factually: Notice what is happening in the moment around positive social norms without blame or judgement.
Connect & Validate: Acknowledge feelings and safety needs clearly and calmly.
Respond Simply: Choose one clear, age-appropriate action or boundary for positive social norms.
Reflect & Repair: Review what worked, repair any rupture honestly, and record your next small step.
parent_scripts: "I can see this moment feels big right now. Let's slow down and take one step together with positive social norms."
"Everyone is safe here. We can talk about what happened and work out the next step calmly."
"I noticed I was getting stressed. I'm taking a breath so I can listen properly."
"We don't have to get everything perfect today — we are practising positive social norms one routine at a time."
practical_examples: Everyday Routine: Applying positive social norms during a busy morning or bedtime transition by slowing down, offering two calm choices, and keeping tone steady.
Moment of Stress: When tension rises around positive social norms, pausing for 10 seconds before speaking, validating feelings, and focusing on safety first.
Follow-Through & Review: Recording a factual note after practising positive social norms to notice what helped the child settle and what support would help next time.
reflection_questions: What part of positive social norms feels easiest for me?
What part feels hardest, and why?
How did my own childhood shape my reactions?
What is one small change I can try this week?
practice_ideas: Try a 2-minute grounding exercise before responding to your child.
Practice naming emotions using simple, non-judgemental language.
Role-play a challenging moment and rehearse a calm script.
Identify one routine where positive social norms can be used daily.
content.closing_message: Progress in positive social norms comes from small, consistent moments of safety, honesty, and repair — not perfection. Every time you pause, stay regulated, and choose a safer response, you build lasting trust.

content_variants.toddlers: For babies & toddlers (0–4): Focus on gentle tone, physical comfort, predictable routines, and simple 3-to-5 word reassurance while practising positive social norms.
content_variants.school_age: For school-age children (5–11): Use clear explanations, visual routines, curiosity about their feelings, and collaborative problem-solving around positive social norms.
content_variants.teens: For adolescents (12–18): Respect autonomy, listen without lecturing, agree on clear safety boundaries, and involve teens in decisions about positive social norms.
content_variants.fatherhood: For fathers & male caregivers: Model calm accountability, steady emotional presence, and non-frightening leadership when practising positive social norms.

red_flags: Immediate physical danger, threats, intimidation, or coercive control observed during positive social norms.
A child shows fear, freezing, dissociation, or disclosure of harm related to positive social norms.
An adult is unable to regulate or maintain safe supervision while attempting positive social norms.
Signs of acute mental health crisis or substance intoxication affecting child safety.
when_to_escalate: Pause learning immediately if anyone is in danger and use verified emergency or crisis supports.
Follow jurisdiction-specific child protection and mandatory reporting obligations when harm is disclosed or suspected.
Engage a qualified supervisor, specialist DFV practitioner, or clinician when risk exceeds self-directed learning.

trauma_informed.clinical: Nervous-system lens for positive social norms: Recognises fight, flight, freeze, and fawn survival responses, window of tolerance, and the need for co-regulation before cognitive problem-solving.
trauma_informed.relational: Attachment lens for positive social norms: Prioritises connection before correction, attunement to cues, shame-free accountability, and timely repair after ruptures.
trauma_informed.justice: Fairness & cultural lens for positive social norms: Respects cultural strengths, kinship networks, neurodiversity, disability access, and structural barriers without equating poverty with neglect.
trauma_informed.fatherhood: Accountable fatherhood lens for positive social norms: Replaces control or withdrawal with steady, reliable care, honest repair, and child-centred safety.

sections.simplified_parent_version:
What positive social norms means:
Positive Social Norms is about keeping daily life safe, calm, and predictable so your child feels supported and understood.

How to practise it:
1. Pause and take one slow breath first.
2. Notice what your child needs right now.
3. Use a calm voice and one clear step.
4. Repair kindly if things go off track.

How trauma and stress impact behaviour.
How parents can model emotional regulation.
